name: Thangal Naga
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: The phonological system of Thangal consists of twenty one consonant sounds, twelve vowels sounds of which six pure vowels and six diphthongs under segmental phoneme, and two supra-segmental phonemes (i.e., two tones as level and falling). [p. 18] ... Being a Tibeto-Burman language, Thangal also has the tonal system. There are two tones in Thangal, viz. (a) falling tone and (b) level tone. Level tone is not marked here and falling tone is indicated by the mark /ˋ/. [p. 46] To my findings, following mono syllabic and disyllabic words which has tone and they are all marked, there is no tone in every word in Thangal. [p. 47]
new_statements.citation: Thokchom Chandramani Singh (2008). The Structural Analysis of Thangal. Ph.D. thesis, Department of Linguistics, Manipur University, Canchipur, May 2008. Chapter II, The Phonological System.
new_statements.locator: Ch. II §2.0, thesis p. 18 (scan p. 2 of); §2.4 Tones, thesis pp. 46-47 (scan pp. 30-31)
new_statements.rule_in_words: The source treats Thangal as a two-tone language (level vs falling, contrastive in monosyllables and disyllables, e.g. /sona/ 'snake' vs /sonà/ 'coin') and lists tone as the only suprasegmental phoneme type; it makes no statement about word stress or accent anywhere in the phonology chapter (syllable section covers structure, types, CV patterns and syllabification only). No stress placement rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone the author notes that not every word carries (marked) tone ('there is no tone in every word in Thangal', p. 47).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level description (monosyllabic and disyllabic citation forms in the tone lists); the falling-tone mark is transcribed by the author from scanned ('/*/' in scanned, a grave-type mark in the scan). Data from Thangal Surung village, Senapati district (ch. I §1.8).
new_statements.identity_note: Singh 2008 describes 'Thangal', explicitly equating it with Khoirao/Koirao (ch. I p. 2 fn. 3: 'Khoirao/Koirao is the synonymous term of Thangal'); data collected at Thangal Surung village, Senapati district, Manipur (ch. I §1.8). Same languoid as than1255 (ISO nki); no dialect split is described.

II §2.0 (p. 18): the phonological system has 33 segmental phonemes 'and two supra-segmental phonemes (i.e., two tones as level and falling)'; §2.4 Tones (pp. 46-47): two tones, level (unmarked) and falling (marked), with minimal pairs; syllable section (§2.3, pp. 39-45) covers syllable types and patterns only. scanned grep of ch. I and II for stress/accent/prominence: no hit. Ch. I p. 16 says ch. II covers 'syllable and tone of the language'.
Names/classification only; the five descriptive references are those in the target record.
No phonology content; further reading lists Singh 2008 and McDonough 2022 only.
